'''Earl Ray Tomblin''' (born March 15, 1952) is an American politician who served as the 35th [[governor of West Virginia]] from 2011 to 2017. A member of the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]], he previously served in the [[West Virginia Senate]] from 1980 to 2011 and as [[president of the West Virginia Senate]] from 1995 to 2011. Tomblin became acting governor in November 2010 following [[Joe Manchin]]'s election to the U.S. Senate. He won a [[2011 West Virginia gubernatorial special election|special election]] in October 2011 to fill the unexpired term ending on January 14, 2013, and was [[2012 West Virginia gubernatorial election|elected]] to a full term as governor in November 2012.

==Early life and education==
Tomblin was born in [[Logan County, West Virginia]], and is the son of Freda M. (née Jarrell) and Earl Tomblin. His mother was 18 years old when he was born.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/southernwv/obituary.aspx?n=freda-mae-tomblin&pid=173187216&fhid=30019|title=Freda Mae Tomblin's Obituary on Southern WV|website=Southern WV|access-date=2018-08-11}}</ref> He has a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree from [[West Virginia University]] where he was a member of [[Kappa Alpha Order]] and then went along to receive a [[Master of Business Administration]] degree from [[Marshall University]].<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |title=Earl Ray Tomblin |url=http://wvencyclopedia.org/articles/2313 |encyclopedia=The West Virginia Encyclopedia |publisher=West Virginia Humanities Council |location=[[Charleston, West Virginia]] |date=November 3, 2010 |access-date=February 8, 2011}}</ref>

==State Legislature and Senate President==
Tomblin was elected to the [[West Virginia House of Delegates]] in 1974, and reelected in 1976 and 1978. He won election to the Senate for the [[West Virginia's 7th Senate district|7th district]] in 1980 and was subsequently re-elected every four years until his election as governor.

Tomblin was elected on January 3, 1995, as the 48th President of the West Virginia Senate. Having served in the position for almost seventeen years, he is the longest serving [[List of Presidents of the West Virginia Senate|Senate President]] in West Virginia's history. Tomblin became the first Lieutenant Governor of West Virginia upon creation of the honorary designation in 2000.

As a senator, he represented the 7th Senate District encompassing [[Boone County, West Virginia|Boone]], [[Lincoln County, West Virginia|Lincoln]], Logan, and [[Wayne County, West Virginia|Wayne]] counties.<ref>{{cite web |title=West Virginia Senate District Map|url=http://www.legis.state.wv.us/districts/sd/sd.cfm|publisher=[[West Virginia Senate]] |access-date=November 28, 2010}}</ref>

===Acting governor===
Tomblin became acting governor when Joe Manchin resigned after [[United States Senate special election in West Virginia, 2010|being elected]] to fill the [[United States Senate]] seat of the late Senator [[Robert Byrd]]. Tomblin is the first person to serve as acting governor under West Virginia's current [[West Virginia Constitution|constitution]].

While acting governor, Tomblin also retained the title of Senate President, per the state constitution.<ref>{{cite web|title=West Virginia Constitution|url=http://www.legis.state.wv.us/WVCODE/WV_CON.cfm|publisher=[[West Virginia Legislature]] |access-date=November 15, 2010}}</ref> However, he did not participate in legislative business or preside over the Senate while acting governor.

==Governor of West Virginia==

===Elections===

====2011 special====
{{main|2011 West Virginia gubernatorial special election}}

Under the [[Constitution of West Virginia|West Virginia constitution]], when the governorship becomes vacant with more than one year remaining in the term, a special election must be held for the remainder of the term. In Manchin's case, he left office two years into his second term. Tomblin stated his desire to run for the remainder of the term. Following a ruling by the [[West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals|Supreme Court of Appeals]] on January 18, 2011, a special gubernatorial election was scheduled for October 4, 2011.<ref>{{cite news |title=Tomblin succeeds Manchin as West Virginia governor|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2010/11/15/AR2010111506129.html |newspaper=Washington Post|date=November 15, 2010|access-date=November 17, 2010}}{{dead link|date=June 2021|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Acting W.Va. Governor Proclaims Oct. 4 Election |url=http://www.wvgazette.com/ap/ApTopStories/201101210972 |newspaper=Charleston Gazette|date=January 21, 2011|access-date=January 21, 2011|url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110622093234/http://www.wvgazette.com/ap/ApTopStories/201101210972 |archive-date=June 22, 2011}}</ref> Tomblin was successful in the Democratic primary, beating a field of six contenders, while Morgantown businessman [[Bill Maloney]] emerged as the Republican nominee in the May 14 primary. Tomblin went on to win the general election against Maloney and was sworn in as governor on November 13, 2011.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://hosted.ap.org/dynamic/files/elections/2011/by_county/WV_Governor_1004.html?SITE=AP&SECTION=POLITICS |title=News from The Associated Press |website=Hosted.ap.org |date=October 5, 2011 |access-date=February 10, 2016}}</ref> Immediately before being sworn in as governor, Tomblin resigned from the state senate.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.wowktv.com/story/16027267/earl-ray-tomblin-to-be-inaugurated-as-west-virginias-governor |title=Earl Ray Tomblin Sworn in as W.Va. Governor – WOWK 13 Charleston, Huntington WV News, Weather, Sports |website=Wowktv.com |access-date=February 10, 2016 |archive-date=April 6, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120406085212/http://www.wowktv.com/story/16027267/earl-ray-tomblin-to-be-inaugurated-as-west-virginias-governor |url-status=dead }}</ref>

====2012====
{{Main|2012 West Virginia gubernatorial election}}
Tomblin ran for re-election to a full term in 2012, and defeated Maloney in a rematch.

===Tenure===
In the [[2016 United States presidential election|2016 presidential election]], Tomblin endorsed fellow Democrat [[Hillary Clinton]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.governor.wv.gov/media/pressreleases/2016/Pages/GOVERNOR-TOMBLIN-ENDORSES-HILLARY-CLINTON-FOR-PRESIDENT.aspx|title=Governor Tomblin Endorses Hillary Clinton for President|publisher=Office of the Governor of West Virginia |date=April 29, 2016|access-date=May 10, 2016|url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160501160315/http://www.governor.wv.gov/media/pressreleases/2016/Pages/GOVERNOR-TOMBLIN-ENDORSES-HILLARY-CLINTON-FOR-PRESIDENT.aspx|archive-date=May 1, 2016}}</ref>

====Abortion====
Tomblin is [[anti-abortion]].<ref name=Foxnews/><ref name=Losangelestimes/> Despite this, in March 2014, Tomblin vetoed a bill that would have banned abortions in West Virginia after 20 weeks, which he said was due to constitutionality issues.<ref name=Foxnews>Associated Press (March 29, 2014) – [https://www.foxnews.com/politics/wv-governor-vetoes-abortion-bill-sparking-outrage-from-national-pro-life-group/ "WV Governor Vetoes Abortion Bill, Sparking Outrage From National Pro-Life Group"]. ''Fox News''. Retrieved March 9, 2015.</ref> In March 2015, Tomblin again vetoed the bill; however, his veto was overridden by the West Virginia legislature.<ref name=Losangelestimes>La Ganga, Maria (March 3, 2015) – [https://www.latimes.com/nation/nationnow/la-na-west-virginia-governor-vetoes-abortion-bill-20150303-story.html "West Virginia Governor Vetoes Bill Banning Abortion At 20 Weeks"]. ''Los-Angeles Times''. Retrieved March 9, 2015.</ref><ref>Eyre, Eric & Nuzum, Lydia (March 6, 2015) – [http://www.wvgazette.com/article/20150306/GZ01/150309374/1101 "20-Week Abortion Ban to Become W.Va. Law; Senate Overrides Tomblin Veto"]. ''The Charleston Gazette''. Retrieved March 9, 2015.</ref>

====Approval ratings====
A May 2013 survey by Republican strategist Mark Blankenship showed Tomblin's job approval rating to be at 69 percent, unchanged from two months earlier.<ref>Kercheval, Hoppy (May 9, 2013) – [http://wvmetronews.com/2013/05/09/poll-numbers-show-manchin-capito-tomblin-tennant-strength/ "Poll Numbers Show Manchin, Capito, Tomblin, Tennant Strength"]. ''WV MetroNews''. Retrieved March 10, 2015.</ref> According to a poll conducted by [[Public Policy Polling]] in September 2013, Tomblin had an approval rating of 47 percent with 35 percent disapproving, up from 44 percent in 2011.<ref>Jensen, Tom (September 25, 2013) – [http://www.publicpolicypolling.com/main/2013/09/west-virginia-miscellany.html#more "West Virginia Miscellany"]. ''Public Policy Polling''. Retrieved March 10, 2015.</ref>

===Term limit===
Tomblin was barred from running for a second full term in 2016. Under the constitution, a partial term counts toward the limit of two consecutive terms.

==Personal life==
Tomblin was married on September 8, 1979, to [[Joanne Tomblin]], a native New Yorker and graduate of Marshall University, who served as the president of [[Southern West Virginia Community and Technical College]] from 1999 to 2015.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.firstlady.wv.gov/pages/biography.aspx |title=About the First Lady |website=Firstlady.wv.gov |date=November 15, 2010 |access-date=February 10, 2016 |archive-date=March 4, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304080834/http://www.firstlady.wv.gov/pages/biography.aspx |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.southernwv.edu/news/president-joanne-jaeger-tomblin-announces-retirement |title=President Joanne Jaeger Tomblin Announces Retirement &#124; News from Southern |website=Southernwv.edu |access-date=February 10, 2016 |archive-date=March 4, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304023154/http://www.southernwv.edu/news/president-joanne-jaeger-tomblin-announces-retirement |url-status=dead }}</ref> They reside in [[Chapmanville, West Virginia|Chapmanville]] and have one son, Brent. Tomblin attends the First Presbyterian Church of Logan.
